I want to write a little bit about the genesis of this project, mostly so that I
don't forget. It may also be useful to some reader to peek behind the curtain of
how professors at liberal arts colleges work.

Part of where this project came from was a random blog post that I was reading
about Murray Edelman, whose concept of "symbolic reassurance" is one of the most
powerful and under-examined concepts in the discipline. I find that it's even
more powerful when considered in his own historical context. I'm liable to get
bogged down if I write any more about Edelman, so I'll try to get to the point.
It's going to take a second.

At the time, I was working in an administrative role at the college and didn't
have time to dedicate to serious scholarship. My curiosity was rather untethered
and I indulged it in spare moments between trying to establish a program in
"public philosophy" and implementation of an expanded, branded "experiential
learning" initiative.

So, when I had time to read a blog post on Murray Edelman, I found stray
references to an unknown-to-me author named Eric Berne and his book *Games
People Play*. The post didn't provide a satisfactory explanation of the connection between Berne and Edelman. And so the reference
was like a fly to a brook trout: a hook in a swiftly moving stream.

Over the next few months, I put the pieces together of who Berne was: a Canadian
who had trained in psychoanalysis and settled in Northern California. It didn't take much: he's reasonably well-documented online. He was
mostly in private practice, not institutional. But he was well-known in his
field as the founder of a therapeutic methodology called "transactional
analysis." *Games People Play* was a mature expression of this methodology. The
book itself, I would learn, is a strange text: part textbook for therapists,
part self-help, and partly a book for the general reader. It seemed
self-conscious and like it was attempting humor, though most of what he seems to
try and pass off as humor are bald-faced misogyny and homophobia. In that
regard, parts of it are hard to get through.

In writing [my paper on John Dewey](https://doi.org/10.1086/685761) I had come across the vocational
guidance literature, so I had a basic mental model of how to understand *Games
People Play*, but not one large enough to shake my curiosity off of it.

That's where the project got its start: a random blog post on an afternoon
between administrative tasks.

But I forgot to mention one thing: *Games People Play* wasn't some obscure text
from the 1960s. It had been a smash for its publisher.
It was well-known enough that in 1968 Joe South released a song called ["Games
People Play,"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vDeVonv3kY0) which won the Grammy for Song of the Year. I'm pretty certain, though I haven't been able to find the documentary connection that I would need to make the claim in academic writing, that South's song is inspired by the book and its popularity. The Grove Press archives may have just what I'm after; a publisher like Grove would want their piece of the pie.

It has been recorded by something like two hundred artists since. King Curtis's
instrumental version (Duane Allman on guitar) won a Grammy of its own. Dolly Parton did a version.  My
favorite is Lee Dorsey's, on [*Yes We
Can*](https://www.discogs.com/release/11864364-Lee-Dorsey-Yes-We-Can) (1970),
produced by the inimitable Allen Toussaint.

As unsexy as that sounds, it's how the project got started. Sometimes the life
of the mind is just another day at the office.
